fields.short: Very common: 76 in 100 people at harm reduction sites said they'd used alone at least once in the past week. The most-picked reason: it's easier and more comfortable at home.
fields.but: It's one survey in one part of Canada, of people who already went to these sites.
how: In 2018, 414 people at 27 sites in British Columbia, Canada, answered a survey. The sites hand out safer-use supplies.
Of those who used alone, 44 in 100 said using at home was easier and more comfortable; 14 in 100 did not want others to know. Some wrote that they had no one to use with.
People who used alone more often had no steady home: 38 in 100, against 24 in 100 of those who didn't.
The survey could not show if using alone changes overdose risk. It cites coroners' reports. They found that about 7 in 10 people who died of an overdose there in 2016 and 2017 were using alone.

how: 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression took psilocybin in a clinic with music. Almost all said it helped at times; about half said it sometimes made things harder.

Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression a week later. But both were measured at the same time, so feeling better may have made them describe the music more warmly.

In a trial of 10 people trying to quit smoking, each had one session with classical music and one with gongs and singing bowls, in random order. How mystical or hard the sessions felt did not clearly differ.
In a US survey, people who linked their hardest trip to music they disliked didn't rate that trip as harder than others did.

how: 613 US adults who had ever used a psychedelic answered one online survey in 2021, looking back over their whole life.
Most were glad they had used psychedelics: 79 in 100 agreed, at least a little.
In the days or weeks after their hardest trip, 7 in 100 said they'd thought of hurting themselves or others, or tried to.

57 in 100 said a problem like worry or poor sleep lasted at least a few days, and put it down to psychedelics. But people who hadn't used them weren't asked, so it's unknown how many would have had these anyway.

fields.but: These are views given after one made-up story, not how people who use drugs are really treated.
how: 1,613 adults online each read one short story about a person called Alex, with the wording chosen at random. People with a drug or mental health diagnosis, or close family with one, couldn't take part.
When Alex's trouble was put down to drug use, not a health concern, readers wanted much more distance and saw Alex as more dangerous. In a pretend money game, they took slightly more from Alex.
Calling it a brain disease instead of a problem made readers think more that genes or illness caused it. Its other effects were small and unclear.

An older study tested labels on about 500 people at mental health conferences. Those whose story called a man a substance abuser, not someone with a substance use disorder, agreed slightly more with blaming and punishing him. It's a shaky result.

lines.reason: But merged into one sentence and made specific: each reader saw one story, and real treatment of people who use drugs was not measured. How 4: the statement only says the authors described the attendees as care providers. The result is readers' agreement with blame and punishment statements, not blame the man received.

fields.but: Every checklist was made for other drugs, and most studies used volunteers, so the numbers can't be applied to everyone who uses ecstasy.
how: In two US surveys of the general public, about 4 in 100 people who had used ecstasy recently met the criteria for dependence. Among clubgoers, young people in detention and volunteers, it was 16 to 22 in 100.
Three small samples gave much higher numbers: 43 to 73 in 100 met the criteria at some point in their lives. They included people in drug treatment and people who had taken at least 250 pills.
The one study that followed people found that 93 in 100 of those dependent at the start no longer were after about three years. That group was small: about 12 to 14 people, by our count.

The symptoms reported most included carrying on despite problems, lots of time using or recovering, tolerance and withdrawal. Pills sold as ecstasy may hold methamphetamine, so some of this may be dependence on another drug.

lines.reason: But said 'most studies' used forms made for other drugs, but the review says all instruments were; 'may not fit' also softened 'cannot be applied'. How 1: the claim says household (general-population) surveys, not national. Short and the rest faithful.
